st.headline: Why is it so hard talking to your friends about money? A financial expert explains
st.teaser: Talking to friends about money can be sensitive, here’s how to navigate it.
fullText: Synopsis: Every first and third Monday of the month, get a head start in your personal finance, career and life with The Straits Times.
Friendships may be priceless, but money talk often crops up among friends - who owes who money, choosing dinner locations, trying to budget for travel together.
But how can we talk openly about money without breaking friendships?
In this episode, ST business correspondent Sue-Ann Tan and See Kai Wen talk about how to navigate this issue.
Their guest is Vivienne Ong from MoneyOwl.

cna.headline: The hidden dangers behind India’s viral ‘snowy’ tourist spot
cna.teaser: A 350-acre white expanse of marble waste in Kishangarh, western India, has become an unlikely tourist destination.
fullText: KISHANGARH, India: In India’s western state of Rajasthan, a vast white expanse draws thousands of visitors each day. At first glance, the 350-acre site resembles a wintry, snow-covered landscape complete with gleaming ridges.
But this winter wonderland is far from natural. It is, in fact, a dumping ground for marble slurry waste produced by the Kishangarh region’s marble processing facilities.

In recent years, the site has become an unlikely tourist attraction, with mostly domestic visitors travelling from across India to capture unique photographs. Some have likened it to Switzerland, while others say it reminds them of Santorini in Greece.

“My son has visited this place a couple of times. He said it’s very beautiful and insisted I must come,” said Jameel Ahmad Abdul Hameed Moomin, who travelled from Maharashtra with his family to experience the unusual scenery at the Kishangarh marble dumping yard.

The area even has its own Google Maps listing as a tourist attraction, called “Dumping Yard Kishangarh”, boasting a 4.4-star rating from more than 6,800 reviews. Reviewers praised its surreal landscape and shared tips on the best times to visit.
The site has also become a social media sensation, with influencers and photographers helping propel it to viral fame.

Several local businesses are cashing in on the hype, promoting the site as a unique destination for pre-wedding photo and video shoots. Some packages even include horse rides as part of the experience.
But beneath the dazzling spectacle – and in the air around it – the same site is facing scrutiny over pollution, groundwater quality and its impact on nearby villages.

Every day, nearly 2 million liters of marble slurry waste, carried in by hundreds of trucks, is dumped at the yard. Yet visitors, seemingly unaware of – or unbothered by – the potential health risks, continue posing for photographs as trucks unload fresh waste in full view. Some even lie directly on the marble slurry deposits for pictures.

Researchers say the fine marble dust can cause respiratory diseases and other health issues, and turn the surrounding area into an unlivable wasteland. “There is a significant increase in calcium carbonate levels … Over time, the land has turned barren and lost fertility, and the water has developed high TDS (Total Dissolved Solids), making it unfit for drinking,” said Subroto Dutta, head of the department of environmental science at Maharshi Dayanand Saraswati University.

For the city of Kishangarh, the beauty of the gleaming white plateaus comes at a steep cost. Over 200,000 industry workers and nearby residents are regularly exposed to the contamination, a 2022 study by the Central University of Rajasthan found.

“In our village, the fluoride level in the water is high. Because of this, the soil is hardening and crop production has gone down. Children and elderly people are also facing health problems,” said local resident Mona Gujjar.
A February 2025 study on a similar marble waste dump yard elsewhere in Rajasthan revealed potential asbestos exposure.
Asbestos is a naturally occurring fibrous mineral which can become airborne when marble is processed. Inhaling dust containing asbestos can pose serious health risks, including lung cancer.
In Kishangarh, workers at the dump yard usually cover their faces with towels or masks and shield their eyes with sunglasses, while tourists and their children explore the site unmasked.

Researchers say the landfill is being run without proper safeguards to protect human health and the environment, and have criticised the lack of warning signs alerting tourists to the potential risks.
The Kishangarh Marble Association said it has not received any health-related complaints and maintains that the dumpsite has not affected surrounding agricultural land.

When contacted by CNA, Rajasthan state officials did not comment on the concerns, except to note that they would be drawing up new guidelines to prevent unregulated dumping, and action would be taken against violations.

Beyond regulatory action, environmental experts and locals have called for the wastewater generated in marble and granite cutting to be treated and recycled, rather than discharged into open dumping sites.

listening.title: Singapore accelerates electric vehicle charging network
listening.transcript: As Singapore moves closer to its green goals, more housing estates are seeing the installation of electric vehicle charging points. The Land Transport Authority aims to install sixty thousand charging points across the island by 2030. Residents are welcoming this initiative, though some express concerns over parking spaces being occupied by non-EV users.

economistArticle.title: Oil prices remain highly flammable
paras: The geopolitical landscape of the Middle East has once again become a tinderbox, sending shockwaves through global energy markets. For months, analysts had assumed that a delicate balance of supply and demand would keep crude oil prices trading in a comfortable band. Yet, recent escalations in the Red Sea and fears of wider conflict have shattered this complacency. Oil prices remain highly flammable, and the prospect of crude returning to triple digits is no longer a distant theoretical threat.

The immediate trigger for the price volatility lies in the precarious shipping lanes of the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea. Tankers are increasingly shunning these vital arteries, opting instead for the lengthy and exorbitant detour around the Cape of Good Hope. This logistical shift not only delays deliveries but also pushes maritime insurance premiums to astronomical heights. As transportation costs surge, the structural vulnerability of the global energy grid is laid bare, proving that modern supply chains are only as strong as their most volatile transit points.

These supply-side disruptions reverberate far beyond the oil terminals, threatening to derail the delicate economic recoveries of major economies. Central banks, particularly the US Federal Reserve, have spent the last two years raising interest rates to quell inflation. A sustained spike in oil prices would undermine these efforts, driving up fuel costs and subsequently the price of goods and services. If energy costs entrench themselves at elevated levels, central bankers may find themselves forced to maintain higher rates for longer, flirting with the risk of global stagflation.

Furthermore, the capricious nature of current OPEC+ policy complicates the picture. While the cartel has pledged production cuts to prop up prices, its internal cohesion is constantly tested by members seeking to maximize short-term revenue. This creates an unpredictable supply environment. If commercial inventories continue to dwindle against a backdrop of geopolitical anxiety, the market could experience a sudden, asymmetric price jump, leaving import-dependent nations in Asia and Europe severely exposed.

Ultimately, the current oil market dynamics serve as a stark reminder of the world’s continued dependency on fossil fuels. Despite the rapid progress of the green energy transition, global industry and transport still run on oil. Any spark in the Middle East has the potential to ignite an economic firestorm that reaches consumers at petrol pumps worldwide. Until alternative energy sources can fully shoulder the burden of global demand, crude oil will remain both a vital economic lubricant and a highly volatile geopolitical weapon.
economistArticle.cn:
中东的地缘政治局势再次成为火药桶，向全球能源市场注入了冲击波。几个月来，分析师们一直认为，供需之间微妙的平衡会将原油价格维持在一个舒适的区间内。然而，最近红海局势的升级以及对更广泛冲突的担忧，打破了这种自满情绪。石油价格依然极易燃烧，原油价格重回三位数的可能性已不再是遥远的理论威胁。

价格波动的直接诱因在于波斯湾和红海不安全的航道。油轮越来越多地避开这些至关重要的交通要道，转而选择绕行好望角，这一路线不仅漫长且费用高昂。这种物流上的转变不仅推迟了交付，还将海上保险保费推向了天文数字。随着运输成本飙升，全球能源网络的结构性脆弱性暴露无遗，这证明了现代供应链的强度取决于其最具波动性的运输节点。

这些供应端的扰动其影响远远超出了石油终端，威胁到主要经济体脆弱的经济复苏。各大央行，尤其是美联储，过去两年一直在提高利率以平息通胀。石油价格的持续飙升将破坏这些努力，推高燃料成本，并随之推高商品和服务的价格。如果能源成本在高位固化，央行行长们可能会发现自己被迫在更长时间内维持较高利率，从而面临全球滞胀的风险。

此外，当前欧佩克+（OPEC+）政策的多变性使局势更加复杂。虽然该卡特尔承诺通过减产来支撑价格，但其内部凝聚力不断受到寻求短期收入最大化的成员国的考验。这创造了一个不可预测的供应环境。如果在地缘政治焦虑的背景下商业库存继续减少，市场可能会经历突然的、非对称的价格暴涨，使亚洲和欧洲依赖进口的国家承受巨大风险。

归根结底，当前的石油市场动态严酷地提醒着人们，世界对化化石燃料的持续依赖。尽管绿色能源转型取得了快速进展，但全球工业和交通仍依赖石油运行。中东的任何火星都有可能点燃一场经济风暴，波及全球加油站前的消费者。在替代能源能够完全承担全球需求的重任之前，原油将既是至关重要的经济润滑剂，也是一种极具波动性的地缘政治武器。

gems.s: As transportation costs surge, the structural vulnerability of the global energy grid is laid bare, proving that modern supply chains are only as strong as their most volatile transit points.
gems.why: This sentence uses the idiom 'laid bare' to expose a weakness, combined with a powerful comparative structure ('only as strong as') that highlights the weakest link metaphor. / 该句使用了成语 'laid bare'（暴露无遗）来揭示弱点，并结合了一个强有力的比较结构（'only as strong as'，即取决于最弱的一环），形象地展现了木桶效应。
